messages.subject: Re: Repeated transects - same day
messages.body_plain:
Carlos, you cannot treat the lines as replicates in such a design, nor can =
you treat a repeat run of the same transect as a separate line.  In the lat=
ter case, you can record effort as line length multiplied by the number of =
times the line was covered, and pool the data on detections.  In the former=
 case, your inference is really restricted to the strips you surveyed - you=
 don't have a basis for extrapolating density to a wider area.  These issue=
s are covered in the introduction to distance sampling book.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject_clean: Constant of proportionality for detection function
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,=20

I'm doing a simulation study and try to thin a Log-Gaussian Cox Process =
using
the detection function which I fitted to the data from my field work.
The detection function is the half normal key + cosine series expansion, =
i.e.
g(y) is proportional to key(y)*(1+series(y)) (Buckland et al. 2001, Eq.
2.25).

My idea was to use 1 / key(0)*(1+series(0)) as constant of =
proportionality,
but I found that this is not the way it is done in DISTANCE.

My problem is, that I do not find an explanation how the constant of
proportionality is calculated in DISTANCE. Maybe someone can tell me how =
it
is done?!

Best regards,=20
Tim	  =20

--

messages.subject: Re: Constant of proportionality for detection function
messages.subject_clean: Constant of proportionality for detection function
messages.body_plain:
Tim, as Distance uses maximum likelihood estimation, you need to work with =
the probability density function, not the detection function.  The constant=
 is then determined by ensuring that the pdf integrates to one.  However, i=
f you want the estimated detection function for line transect sampling, you=
 simply rescale the fitted pdf, so that the function equals 1 at y=3D0 - wh=
ich is equivalent to what you say.  So if you have the fit of key(y)*(1+ser=
ies(y)), rescaling your way will give the fitted detection function.  For p=
oint transect sampling, this doesn't work though, as the pdf and detection =
functions have different shapes.  (The pdf is proportional to y times the d=
etection function.)

If this doesn't answer your query, perhaps we can sort it off the list?

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: Stratification Help
messages.body_plain:
Justus:

I wish I could show you the 'stratification command' in Distance.
Unfortunately there is no such thing for the multilayer survey that you
have carried out.

I suggest you poke around within the archives of this list for
inspiration.  You will need to alter your problem in some manner
(combine 2 seasons by 2 sites into 4 season-site strata; invoke
something as a covariate for your detection function modelling perhaps)
to be able to make progress.  We can't offer usable advice beyond this.
Have a look at an extensive comment Jeff Laake provided on this subject
back in 2008
https://www.jiscmail.ac.uk/cgi-bin/webadmin?A2=ind0805&L=DISTANCE-SAMPLING&P=R807&1=DISTANCE-SAMPLING&9=A&J=on&d=No+Match%3BMatch%3BMatches&z=4.
Or put in your own search term in the archive search engine
(https://www.jiscmail.ac.uk/cgi-bin/webadmin?A0=DISTANCE-SAMPLING)

See if that doesn't get you started on your search.

messages.subject: Re: measuring distances when horizon is not available
messages.subject_clean: measuring distances when horizon is not available
messages.body_plain:
A clinometer will work at very close distances but once the angle is
smallish (<5 degrees) they aren't very useful. A less expensive laser
range finder will do better than a clinometer.  Alternatively if you can
get the distance to the iceberg (radar?)at the time of the measurement
you can still use it in place of the horizon distance with reticle
binoculars.

--jeff

messages.subject: Line-transect Analysis - Segmented Transect question
messages.body_plain:
Hello-

I am analyzing ship-based line transect data for Marine mammals, and have=
 numerous transects (defined as a line  traversing the study site) that a=
re segmented, usually because poor weather or other constraints prevented=
 us from completing them.  The study area is large (>600,000 km 2) and mo=
st 'planned' transects were several hundred km long, but in some cases on=
ly a fraction of these were presented.=20

A related issue is that some of the completed  'transects' actually ended=
 up being zig-zag courses within the study area.=20

My questions are:
1) is there a minimum lenght (or proportion of planned transects) that sh=
ould be considered a transect when analyzing the data in Distance?
2) if yes to above, can I combine segments to make a transect of sufficen=
t length 'after the fact'?
3) are there any issues with using zig-zag transects (assuming we can acc=
ount for re-sighting of the same individuals) as opposed to 'line' transe=
ct, within in the study site (I define a 'zig-zag transect' as a single t=
ransect that has a zig-zag pattern to it).

Thank you,
-Tom N.

--

messages.subject: Re: Line-transect Analysis - Segmented Transect question
Adjusted Angle Zig Zag design
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Currently designing boat based surveys for seabirds with a set survey
budget, and in a vigorous tidal environment, and so I'm proposing to  use a
zig zig survey pattern.  Given the survey effort available, strong
patterning is apparent when using equal-spaced transects, so I'm proposing
to use adjusted-angle samplers, approximated by straight lines (this looks
reasonable). Usually Distance  can successfully generate survey routes using
this design, but sometimes  its fails generating this error message:

** Error: Problems generating the adjusted angle zigzag sampler. Too little
effort for the survey region height of 680.22458243079. Try increasing the
survey effort, adjusting the design angle or changing the stratification.
**

Because the generation of some survey route instances is unsuccessful, this
prevents Distances estimating coverage for the design. I am reluctant to
adopt any of the proposed solutions as my survey effort /design angle are
relatively fixed, and there's no obvious way to change the stratification.

So:

*   Can I assume even coverage for the design without testing this?

*   Can  assume that a route randomly chosen for the instances which are
successfully generated is valid, or does the fact that some instances are
not successfully generated violate the underlying assumptions?

*   Should I stick with the adjusted angle design, or revert to even
spacing?

Also, in some instances the first and/or last transects are much shorter
than the other transects. I'm wondering if for the purposes of design based
estimates I can combine these short transects with their neighbours so as to
reduce the variance of my encounter rate estimate, or by doing this would I
be violating some key underlying assumption.

Any help gratefully appreciated.

Many thanks.

Nigel Harding

--

messages.subject: Stratified verse unstratified
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am having trouble understanding how stratified and
unstratified designs given the same data and same transect lengths could
produce very different results. The difference in density estimates is quiet
large, around 15% in each case. My understanding was unstratified sampling given
same data should produce similar results as model averaging should produce a similar
detection function to stratified sampling, where detection function is estimated
for each strata. Maybe I have done something wrong, because I am struggling to explain
why stratified results consistently estimate more animals than unstratified.
Any help appreciated.

Brett

--

PhD Candidate
Fenner School of Environment and Society
ANU College of Medicine, Biology & Environment
The Australian National University
